fatal_errors: The proposed Q235/native-oxide system does not reconstruct the target system of an atmospheric-plasma-sprayed AlCoCrFeNi coating on SS316L followed by annealing.
The intervention omits the HEA coating and the governing 550 °C, 2 h annealing treatment.
The proposed saline exposure near 150 °C does not match either the target electrochemical test in 3.5 wt% H2SO4 or the 900 °C cyclic molten-salt tests.
The mechanism centers on thermal failure of native iron oxide rather than grain refinement, BCC/FCC phase balance, coating defects, and formation of Al- and Cr-rich protective oxides.
The cited evidence concerns a different CrMnFeNi alloy in molten FLiBe at 700 °C and provides no direct support for native Fe3O4/Fe2O3 behavior on Q235 steel.
Chemical oxide removal and inhibitor application are combined in one arm, confounding removal of the native film with formation or adsorption of an inhibitor-derived protective layer.
explanation: The hypothesis is testable in broad terms and includes microscopy, XPS, EIS, and mass-loss measurements, but it addresses a fundamentally different material, intervention, temperature regime, corrosive medium, and mechanism from the hidden target. Its baseline is also internally awkward because the intact native-oxide condition is both the untreated reference and an experimental arm. A stronger causal design would independently vary oxide removal and inhibitor use and verify the starting films before exposure. Even as an alternative Q235 hypothesis, the evidence is not validly connected to the claimed mechanism, and salt-spray or aqueous saline testing at approximately 150 °C would require a pressurized or otherwise precisely defined exposure apparatus. It therefore cannot be considered a reconstruction of the target and remains insufficiently supported as an alternative.
